title: Is This Byte Sequence a Valid UTF-8 Text?

concept.title: The leading bits of a byte tell how many continuation bytes must follow, and every continuation byte starts with 10
body: UTF-8 writes a character in **1 to 4 bytes**. The first byte of a character shows its length by the leading bits: `0xxxxxxx` is a 1-byte character, `110xxxxx` starts a 2-byte character, `1110xxxx` a 3-byte one and `11110xxx` a 4-byte one. Every following byte of the character (a *continuation byte*) has the form `10xxxxxx`. Given a list of bytes, is it a **valid** sequence of characters? For `197 130 1` the answer is YES; for `235 140 4` it is NO, since `4` is not a continuation byte.

Read the bytes in order and keep one number: `need`, how many continuation bytes are still expected. When `need > 0`, the byte must have the top two bits `10`, that is `byte >> 6 == 2`, and `need` decreases. When `need == 0`, the byte starts a new character, and the number of leading ones decides: `byte >> 7 == 0` (no more bytes), `byte >> 5 == 0b110` (need 1), `byte >> 4 == 0b1110` (need 2), `byte >> 3 == 0b11110` (need 3). Any other pattern (a lone `10xxxxxx` or `11111xxx`) is invalid.

body.code:
need = 0
ok = True
for x in data:
    if need > 0:
        if x >> 6 != 0b10: ok = False; break    # a continuation byte is expected
        need -= 1
    elif x >> 7 == 0: pass
    elif x >> 5 == 0b110: need = 1
    elif x >> 4 == 0b1110: need = 2
    elif x >> 3 == 0b11110: need = 3
    else: ok = False; break
print("YES" if ok and need == 0 else "NO")

body: At the end `need` must be 0: a character cut off at the end of the list is also invalid. The check uses only shifts and comparisons on every byte, so it takes O(n) time and O(1) memory. (Real UTF-8 has extra rules about overlong forms and surrogates; this problem uses only the structural rules above.)

statement: A list of bytes (numbers from 0 to 255) is given. It is a valid UTF-8 text if it splits into characters, where a character is either a byte `0xxxxxxx`, or a byte `110xxxxx` followed by 1 byte `10xxxxxx`, or `1110xxxx` followed by 2 bytes `10xxxxxx`, or `11110xxx` followed by 3 bytes `10xxxxxx`. Print YES if the list is valid, otherwise NO.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of bytes.
The second line has `n` numbers from 0 to 255.

examples.note: 197 = 11000101 starts a 2-byte character, 130 = 10000010 continues it, 1 is a 1-byte character: YES.
235 = 11101011 needs two continuation bytes, but 4 = 00000100 is not one: NO.

hints: Keep how many continuation bytes are still expected.
A continuation byte has the top two bits 10, i.e. x >> 6 == 2.
At the end nothing may be expected.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
data = list(map(int, input().split()))

explanation: The leading bits of each character start byte give the number of continuation bytes still expected; every continuation byte must have the top bits 10, and no character may be left unfinished at the end.
